The Earth's gravity well grabs most of the junk in our local system but some does hit the moon. We just can't see it because the impacts are so small.

The largest contributing factor is that the Moon is tidally locked in its orbit. It's "day" (rotation around its own axis) is the same length as its "year" (orbit around the parent body). On the scale of the solar system, most meteors, on average, that are heading towards the Earth-Moon pair that strike the Moon are going to hit the far side because the near side (the side we see) is shielded from meteors by the Earth itself. If we look at the two sides of the Moon, this seems to hold up; the near side has large maria (the dark spots) which are relatively smooth volcanic formations that have mostly gone undisturbed. The far side appears to be far more pocketed from meteor impacts.

And we have seen meteors hit the moon. Here is video captured by a Chinese satellite. You can even see the crater seconds after the impact. Googling "meteor impacts on the moon" spits out lots of results.
